config.title: Berlin Water Hardness - FAQ
config.subtitle: How hard the water really is per postcode, why it scales, what to set on the dishwasher and washing machine, and when a filter is worth it.

items.q: How hard is the water in Berlin?
items.a: Hard everywhere, with real local differences. The nine Berliner Wasserbetriebe waterworks delivered 15,1 to 23,3 °dH as 2025 annual medians, and the official per-postcode network ranges run from about 10,3 up to 25,7 °dH. Every Berlin postcode is classified hart (3), the hard class that starts at 14 °dH.

items.q: Why is Berlin tap water so hard?
items.a: Because it is 100 percent local groundwater. Rain filters slowly through the calcium-rich glacial sand and gravel under Berlin and Brandenburg, dissolving calcium and magnesium on the way. The waterworks remove iron and manganese but do not soften the water, so the minerals arrive at your tap.

items.q: Is hard water safe to drink?
items.a: Yes. Hardness is calcium and magnesium, the same minerals sold in supplements, and Berlin tap water is controlled under the German drinking water ordinance with published analysis values. Hardness says nothing about pollution. The limescale in your kettle is unpleasant for the machine, not for you.

items.q: What hardness setting should my dishwasher use?
items.a: Look up your postcode's official range and set the machine to the upper end, which in most of Berlin means roughly 16 to 25 °dH. Then keep regenerating salt topped up; the salt is what lets the built-in softener work. With the right setting, glasses stop coming out cloudy.

items.q: Do I need a water filter or softener in Berlin?
items.a: Not for safety, and for most kitchens not at all: correct detergent dosing and regular descaling with citric acid handle hard water for a few euros a year. The honest exception is an espresso machine, where scale kills heating blocks; a filter cartridge or filtered water protects an expensive machine.

items.q: How often should I descale a kettle in Berlin?
items.a: With daily use, roughly monthly in most of the city, and faster where the range tops 20 °dH, as in parts of the east and southeast. Citric acid from any drugstore does the job: dissolve, boil briefly, let it sit, rinse. Vinegar works too but leaves a smell in plastic kettles.
